title: No Capitals in the Capital: researchED Canberra Recap
author: thedisruptiveeducator
summary: A recap of the inaugural researchED Canberra conference from an Australian instructional-coaching presenter, weaving together five sessions into a single argument about the gap between knowing good pedagogy and actually implementing it school-wide. Greg Ashman's keynote redefines explicit teaching as a whole instructional system rather than a single explaining step, built from four components culminating in gradual release of responsibility. Jeanette Breen and Jenny Donovan both push writing instruction toward explicit, knowledge-rich sequencing, arguing students cannot write about what they don't know and that writing complexity demands direct teaching rather than incidental pickup. Sarah Siakew's session is the connective tissue: using the analogy of a swan gliding on water, she argues that observable classroom practice is only a thin slice of the knowledge, routines and professional judgment underneath it, and that copying a technique without understanding why it works produces hollow, performative versions of good pedagogy. The piece closes on Ashman's practical change-management tip of piloting new instructional shifts with willing staff in Term 4 rather than launching them cold in January.
points: Ashman's four-part definition of explicit teaching (breaking down complex ideas, teaching and processing each component, high interactivity, gradual release) reframes it as an entire instructional system rather than a single explaining step.

Ashman's practical change-management advice is to pilot new instructional shifts with enthusiastic staff during a Term 4 window rather than launching them cold in January, when goodwill for new initiatives is already exhausted.

Breen's principle that "the learned curriculum is the only curriculum that actually counts" pushes schools to deliberately map the knowledge students must retain, both vertically across year levels and horizontally across subjects, so they have something to write about.

Siakew's "swan on water" analogy explains why copying an instructional technique without the underlying knowledge produces "lethal mutations" — practices that look compliant on an observation checklist but aren't functioning as intended.

Donovan's keynote argues writing instruction must be explicit and systematic because it requires students to coordinate knowledge, grammar, motor skills and genre demands simultaneously — skills that, unlike spoken language, are not innately acquired.
quotes: When I talk about explicit teaching, it is not the point where you explain something; it is the entire system.

Writing relies heavily on knowledge. It's not purely about vocabulary and grammar, but about the content of the writing itself. This means that if we want our students to be able to write successfully, we need to deliberately plan and sequence knowledge across the curriculum in such a way that it gives students something to write about.

Sarah speaks about how as the evidence around practice travels through a system, it encounters friction at each different transition point. Even the movement from school leaders to heads of faculty to classroom teachers introduces at least two transitions where that information can be diluted or changed.

Sarah used the analogy of a swan on water, emphasising that focusing only on what we can observe in a lesson misses everything beneath it: the teacher knowledge, professional learning, routines and the several hundred decisions that teacher is making every moment.

It requires students to coordinate knowledge, grammar, motor skills and the demands of genre, all whilst managing the known limitations of working memory. And unlike spoken language, many of these things cannot be innately acquired by students.
AERO's work uncovered three central problems in writing instruction: insufficient time dedicated to writing instruction, insufficient frequency of practice and insufficient pedagogical knowledge.
It never ceases to amaze me that a grassroots movement built around getting research into classrooms in a way that is genuinely accessible to teachers has made its way all the way here to Australia.
